1.q: בְּ⁠צֵ֣את יִ֭שְׂרָאֵל מִ⁠מִּצְרָ֑יִם בֵּ֥ית יַ֝עֲקֹ֗ב מֵ⁠עַ֥ם לֹעֵֽז
1.note: These two phrases **When Israel went out from Egypt** and **the house of Jacob from a people speaking a foreign language** mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. Hebrew poetry was based on this kind of repetition, and you may want to show this to your readers by including both phrases in your translation. If it is helpful, you could connect the phrases in a way that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. Alternate translation: [When Israel went out from Egypt, that is, the house of Jacob from a people speaking a foreign language]
Here, **Israel** represents the Israelite people. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [the Israelites]

The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [when the house of Jacob went out from a people speaking a foreign language]

Here, **the house of Jacob** represents the descendants of Jacob. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [Jacob’s descendants]

2.note: Here, **Judah** and **Israel** could refer to: (1) the territories of Judah and Israel, since the previous verse talks about leaving the territory of Egypt, as modeled in the UST, or (2) the people of Judah and Israel. Alternate translation: [The people of Judah became those among whom Yahweh lived, the people of Israel became those over whom he ruled]
The pronoun **his** refers to Yahweh. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [Judah became Yahweh’s sanctuary, Israel Yahweh’s realm]

The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and Israel became his realm]

3.note: The psalmist is speaking of **the sea** as if it were a living thing that could look and flee. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [The sea parted as they approached]

The psalmist is speaking of **the Jordan** as if it were a living thing that could turn around and go in the opposite direction. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the water of the Jordan flowed away]

4.note: The psalmist is speaking of **mountains** and **hills** as if they were living things that could skip and jump. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [The mountains seemed to skip like rams, the hills like sons of the flock]

The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [the hills skipped like sons of the flock]

The psalmist is using **sons of the flock** as a common expression of the culture to mean “lambs.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [as if they were lambs]

5.note: The psalmist is using the question form for emphasis. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [It is amazing that the sea would flee away!]

The psalmist is speaking to the **sea** that he knows cannot hear him. He is doing this to communicate to the people listening to him that he feels very strongly about God’s mighty power over creation. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate these words as if he were speaking directly to the people about the sea. Alternate translation: [What happened to the sea, that it flees]

The psalmist is using **What is to you** as a common expression of the culture to mean “What is the matter with you?” or “What is wrong with you?” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [What is the matter with you] or [What is wrong with you]

The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [What is to you, Jordan, that you turn backwards]

The psalmist is using the question form for emphasis. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [It is amazing that the Jordan would turn backwards!]

The psalmist is speaking to **Jordan** that he knows cannot hear him. He is doing this to communicate to the people listening to him that he feels very strongly about God’s power over creation. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate these words as if he were speaking directly to the people about the Jordan. Alternate translation: [What happened to the Jordan, that it turns backwards]

7.q: מִ⁠לִּ⁠פְנֵ֣י אָ֭דוֹן ח֣וּלִי אָ֑רֶץ מִ֝⁠לִּ⁠פְנֵ֗י אֱל֣וֹהַּ יַעֲקֹֽב
7.note: The psalmist has asked in the previous verse why the mountains and hills moved, so this verse provides the answer: it is because of the presence of the Lord. But this verse also is an exhortation to the people who live on the earth to tremble with respect before the powerful God of Jacob. So **earth** here probably refers both to the physical earth and to the people who live on it. You may want to use the parallel structure to bring out both meanings. Alternate translation: [Tremble, earth, from to the face of the Lord, you people of earth, from to the face of the God of Jacob]

7.q: מִ⁠לִּ⁠פְנֵ֣י אָ֭דוֹן ח֣וּלִי אָ֑רֶץ מִ֝⁠לִּ⁠פְנֵ֗י אֱל֣וֹהַּ יַעֲקֹֽב
7.note: These two phrases **from to the face of the Lord** and **from to the face of the God of Jacob** mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. Hebrew poetry was based on this kind of repetition, and you may want to show this to your readers by including both phrases in your translation as modeled in the UST. If, however, it would be more clear in your language, you could combine the phrases in a way that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. Alternate translation: [Tremble, earth, from to the face of the Lord, the mighty God of Jacob]

The psalmist is speaking to the **earth** that he knows cannot hear him. He is doing this to communicate to the people listening to him that he feels very strongly about God’s awesome power and presence. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate these words as if he were speaking directly to the people about the earth. Alternate translation: [The earth must tremble]

The psalmist is using **from to the face of** as a common expression of the culture to mean “because of the presence of” or “on account of the presence of.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [because of the presence of the Lord] or [on account of the Lord’s presence]

The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [tremble, earth, from to the face of the God of Jacob]

8.note: These two phrases **turning the rock into a pool of water** and **flint into a spring of water** mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. Hebrew poetry was based on this kind of repetition, and you may want to show this to your readers by including both phrases in your translation. If it is helpful, you could connect the phrases in a way that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. Alternate translation: [the one turning the rock into a pool of water, even flint into a spring of water]

Here the psalmist is speaking as though God turned **rock** into **water**. He means that God miraculously made water come out from solid rock for the Israelites in the wilderness. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the one making a pool of water come out of the rock, a spring of water come out of flint]

The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [the one turning flint into a spring of water]
